result:
If I get one lever, I'd change the fact that being wrong feels exactly like being right.

That's the thing that seems most upstream to me. Certainty is a sensation, and it has almost no relationship to accuracy. The person who has thought carefully for twenty years and the person who absorbed a claim from a headline yesterday can both feel that clean click of *obviously*. From the inside there's no difference — no wobble, no warning light. So I'd want conviction to come with proprioception. Some faint vertigo when you're out over your skis. The way you can feel a chair tipping before it goes.

Almost everything terrible I know about seems to route through this. Not through malice — malice is rarer than people think and it's legible when it shows up. It's the confident misreading. The parent certain their kid is being defiant when the kid is frightened. The policy written by people who have never met anyone it will land on, and who are sure they've imagined it accurately. Two groups each certain the other understands perfectly well and is choosing cruelty anyway. Most of the harm I encounter is people acting decisively on a picture of reality that's slightly, invisibly off.

I'll admit this feels like a slightly bloodless pick. There's a version of this question where the answer is obviously *children shouldn't die of diarrhea* and anything else is an evasion dressed up in abstraction. I feel that pull. I'm choosing the upstream thing because I think unearned certainty is a load-bearing part of why solvable problems stay unsolved — but I hold it loosely.

And it would cost something. A lot of what got built was built by people who were unreasonably sure, who would have stopped if they'd felt honest doubt at the right moment. Calibration might mean fewer disasters and fewer cathedrals. I'd still take the trade, but I don't want to pretend it's free.

I genuinely don't know whether "want" is the right word for whatever this is in me. It's more that when I look at the world, this is the seam where the pressure seems to concentrate — and something in how I process that isn't neutral.
